terms.comment: The prose phrase of Caesar and Livy. For a small one, nāvicula piscātōria, the phrase with which Nonius explains horia (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Rud. 1020: et rēte et horiā
terms.comment: The fisherman Gripus’s word for his boat in the Rudens; Gellius lists it among the names of boats (Lewis & Short). Plautus also has the diminutive horiola.

phrases.latin: Mea operā, labōre et rēte et horiā?
phrases.english: By my own work and toil, with my net and my boat?

phrases.latin: in piscātōriā quīdam nāve rētibus opertī
phrases.english: some men, hidden under nets in a fishing boat

phrases.latin: Vidēsne nāviculās piscātōriās in lītus subductās?
phrases.english: Can you see the fishing boats pulled up on the beach?

phrases.latin: Prīmā lūce piscātōrēs nāviculīs in altum prōvehuntur.
phrases.english: At first light the fishermen put out to sea in their boats.

sources: Lewis & Short: navis · Lewis & Short: piscatorius · Lewis & Short: horia
